findings.english_quote: against the God who truly is
findings.issue: ὄντως qualifies θεοῦ as genuinely or actually God. The draft instead introduces an existential formulation, explicitly reinforced by its note describing an assertion of actual existence. This shifts the source's qualification of divine identity into a separate assertion that God exists. Mentioning “the true God” as an alternative does not remedy that shift.
findings.suggested_revision: Use “against the real God” or “against the one who really is God.” Revise the lexical rationale to explain the qualification of genuine deity rather than treating ὄντως as an independent existential expression.

findings.source_quote: ἐν ταῖς θεολογίαις ὁ πονηρὸς τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ τὸν θεὸν οὐκ ἔλαττον ἀγαπῶν ἑνὶ μόνῳ ἀπολείπεται τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ
findings.english_quote: The following contrast concerns differing responses to ignorant impiety, supporting generic human character types. Grammatically, “the evil one” and “the good one” remain possible, but those renderings would suggest more specific referents not established by this sentence.
findings.issue: The generic-human interpretation is grammatically possible, but its disclosure does not adequately address the supplied context. Section 3.3 already uses ὁ πονηρός for the figure conducting the testing of human beings, rendered there as “the evil one.” Here the request attributed to wickedness and the subsequent healing and saving functions also materially support a reading involving personal evil and good agents rather than generic human types. The note lists alternative labels but discounts their contextual support by considering only this sentence.
findings.suggested_revision: Expand the note to acknowledge the possible continuity with ὁ πονηρός in 3.3 and explain the contextual case for personal evil/good agents. Reassess the human-type choice against that evidence. “The evil one” and “the good one” would preserve the source's labels without identifying their bearers; a retained generic-human rendering needs an explicitly contextual rationale and an honest account of the competing reading.
